''Moniera cuneifolia'' Michx. }} '''''Bacopa monnieri''''', also known as '''water hyssop''', '''brahmi''', '''thyme-leafed gratiola''', '''herb of grace''', and '''Indian pennywort''', is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]], creeping [[herb]] native to [[wetland]] areas globally. It is used in [[Ayurveda]]. In 2019, the US [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA) warned manufacturers of [[dietary supplement]] products containing ''Bacopa monnieri'' against making illegal and unproven claims that the herb can treat various diseases. There is inconclusive evidence of it improving cognitive performance and [[memory]], and its safety and effectiveness remain uncertain.{{Cite web |title=Bacopa monnieri: Dietary supplements for brain health |url=https://www.opss.org/article/bacopa-monnieri-dietary-supplements-brain-health |access-date=2025-05-20 |website=www.opss.org |language=en}} ==Description== [[File:Bacopa monnieri W IMG 1612.jpg|thumb|190px|right|''Bacopa monnieri'' in [[Hyderabad]], India]] ''Bacopa monnieri'' is a non-aromatic herb. The [[Leaf|leaves]] of this plant are succulent, oblong, and {{convert|4–6|mm|abbr=on}} thick. Leaves are [[oblanceolate]] and are arranged oppositely on the stem. The [[flower]]s are small, [[actinomorphic]] and white, with four to five petals. It can even grow in slightly [[salinity|brackish]] conditions. Propagation is often achieved through cuttings.{{cite web|last1=Oudhia|first1=Pankaj|title=Bramhi (Bacopa monnieri)|url=https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/CropFactSheets/bramhi.html|publisher=Society for Parthenium Management (SOPAM)|access-date=July 30, 2017|date=2004}} ==Ecology== ''Bacopa monnieri'' is one of the most widespread ''Bacopa'' species. It commonly grows in [[marsh]]y areas throughout [[India]], [[Nepal]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[China]], [[Pakistan]], [[Taiwan]], [[Vietnam]], tropical and southern [[Africa]], on [[Madagascar]], in [[Australia]], in the [[Caribbean]] as well as in Middle and South America. It is also found in [[Florida]], [[Louisiana]], [[Texas]], and [[Hawaii]].{{Cite web |title=Plants of Louisiana |url=https://warcapps.usgs.gov/PlantID/Species/Details/3236 |access-date=2021-07-23 |website=warcapps.usgs.gov}} It used to be found growing wild in freshwater swamps of [[Singapore]] and nearby regions known as ''beremi''.{{Cite magazine |url=https://biblioasia.nlb.gov.sg/vol-17/issue-3/oct-dec-2021/ |title=The Role of Foraging in Malay Cuisine |last=Khir Johari |date=Oct–Dec 2021 |magazine=BiblioAsia |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=20–23 |publisher=National Library Board, Singapore}} ==Research and regulation== ''Bacopa monnieri'' is used in [[Ayurveda|Ayurvedic traditional medicine]] in the belief it may improve memory and various ailments.{{cite journal |last1=Aguiar |first1=Sebastian |last2=Borowski |first2=Thomas |title=Neuropharmacological review of the nootropic herb ''Bacopa monnieri'' |journal=Rejuvenation Research |date=2013 |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=313–326 |doi=10.1089/rej.2013.1431 |pmid=23772955 |pmc=3746283 |issn=1557-8577}} There is no good evidence that it improves cognitive performance and memory, while its safety and effectiveness remain uncertain. In 2019, the FDA issued [[FDA warning letter|warning letters]] to manufacturers of [[dietary supplement]]s containing ''B. monnieri'' that advertised [[health claim]]s for treating or preventing stomach disease, [[Alzheimer's disease]], [[hypoglycemia]], [[blood pressure]], and [[anxiety]] were unproven and illegal.{{cite web |author1=William A Correll, Jr. |title=FDA Warning Letter: Peak Nootropics LLC aka Advanced Nootropics |url=https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/peak-nootropics-llc-aka-advanced-nootropics-565256-02052019 |publisher=Office of Compliance, Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition, Inspections, Compliance, Enforcement, and Criminal Investigations, US Food and Drug Administration |access-date=11 May 2019 |date=5 February 2019}}{{cite web |author1=William A Correll, Jr. |title=FDA Warning Letter: TEK Naturals |url=https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/tek-naturals-565026-02042019 |publisher=Office of Compliance, Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition, Inspections, Compliance, Enforcement, and Criminal Investigations, US Food and Drug Administration |access-date=11 May 2019 |date=5 February 2019}} The FDA stated that no ''B. monnieri'' products have been [[drug approval|approved]] for medical purposes.{{cite web |title=Health fraud scams: Unproven Alzheimer's disease products (''Bacopa monnieri'' listed)|url=https://www.fda.gov/consumers/health-fraud-scams/unproven-alzheimers-disease-products |publisher=US Food and Drug Administration |access-date=11 May 2019 |date=22 December 2018}} ===Adverse effects=== The most commonly reported [[adverse effect]]s of ''B. monnieri'' in humans are [[nausea]], increased [[intestinal motility]], and [[gastrointestinal]] upset. ==Phytochemistry== The best characterized [[phytochemical]]s in ''Bacopa monnieri'' are [[dammarane]]-type [[triterpenoid]] [[saponins]] known as [[bacoside]]s, with jujubogenin or pseudo-jujubogenin [[moiety (chemistry)|moieties]] as [[aglycone]] units.{{cite journal |last1=Sivaramakrishna |first1=C |last2=Rao |first2=CV |last3=Trimurtulu |first3=G |last4=Vanisree |first4=M |last5=Subbaraju |first5=GV |bibcode=2005PChem..66.2719S }} Bacosides comprise a family of 12 known [[structural analog|analogs]].{{cite journal | last1 = Garai | first1 = S | last2 = Mahato | first2 = SB | last3 = Ohtani |
